analyst_notes: The skill version produces a structured output (trimmed draft + numbered diff log + stats block) that the baseline never matches without prompting. The structural assertions (diff log, stats, em-dash check) account for most of the with-skill pass-rate advantage.
Both versions correctly preserved every technical specific across all three test cases. No regressions on accuracy.
The skill version correctly short-circuits on the trivial-tight case; the baseline cannot resist trimming even when no trim is needed. This is the strongest discriminating signal in the eval set.

Word-count floor assertions failed on eval-1 (148 vs 150-240 floor) and eval-2 (63 vs 100-180 floor). The skill cut deeper than the assertion was calibrated for. Audit confirms no technical content was lost in either case; the assertion floors are too tight for inputs that are >60% generic prose. Recalibrate floors in iteration 2 or accept that the skill's own 60% audit threshold is the right governor.

Time cost: with-skill runs are ~13s slower on average (~65% longer) because the skill walks 6 procedure steps. For a one-shot edit, that overhead is fine; for batch edits across a long doc, consider a lighter variant that skips Step 1 classification when invoked repeatedly in the same session.
Token cost: ~19% more tokens with the skill (mostly for the diff log and stats output). This is the cost the skill exists to pay.
